content: Alcohol misuse among young people is a significant concern for various stakeholders, including health services, policymakers, prevention workers, the criminal justice system, youth workers, teachers, and parents. This issue necessitates effective prevention strategies to mitigate its impact. The objective of this review was to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of universal family-based prevention programs in reducing alcohol misuse among school-aged children up to 18 years old. This review also aimed to update a portion of a previously published Cochrane systematic review. The search for relevant studies included evidence up to 2002 from the prior Cochrane review, as well as additional studies published up to July 2010. Databases such as MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, EMBASE, Project CORK, and PsycINFO were utilized to identify relevant literature. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials that evaluated universal family-based prevention programs and reported outcomes related to alcohol use in individuals aged 18 years or younger. Two independent reviewers screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the identified studies to ensure they met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction was conducted independently by two reviewers using a predefined extraction form. The risk of bias in the included studies was also assessed to ensure the reliability of the findings. A total of 12 parallel-group trials were included in the review. However, the overall quality of reporting in these trials was poor. Only 20% of the studies adequately described their methods of randomization and allocation concealment. Approximately half of the trials appropriately addressed incomplete data, while this information was unclear in about 30% of the studies. Due to significant heterogeneity in the interventions, populations, and outcomes, the results were summarized qualitatively rather than quantitatively. Out of the 12 trials, nine demonstrated some evidence of effectiveness when compared to a control or alternative intervention group. These effects were observed to persist over the medium and longer term. Four of the effective interventions specifically targeted young females. One study with a small sample size showed positive effects, but these were not statistically significant. Additionally, two studies with larger sample sizes reported no significant effects of the family-based intervention in reducing alcohol misuse. In conclusion, this Cochrane systematic review found that family-based prevention interventions have small but generally consistent effects in reducing alcohol misuse among young people. These effects are also persistent over the medium to longer term.
